scenes: s01_cold_open
Two hundred and thirteen times every second, a sliver of carbide slams into hardened steel. Each hit steals a little of its edge. And one day, without any warning... it snaps.
s02_title
This is ToolLife Policy. The story of teaching a machine to feel that moment coming. From steel, to signals, to ones and zeros, and back to one simple decision: keep cutting, or change the tool.
s03_wear

Zoom in on a single tooth. A fresh edge slices cleanly. But every hit rubs the face beneath it a little flatter, until the edge stops slicing, and starts pushing. Pushing means more force. More force means more heat. More heat means faster wear. It is a runaway loop, and it ends in fracture.
s04_settings

How long a cutter survives depends on how hard we push it. A wider bite puts more teeth into the steel at once. A longer holder turns the cutter into a diving board: twice as long, up to eight times floppier, until it starts to shake on its own. Our cutters lived anywhere from fifteen to a hundred and fifty cycles.
s05_signals

We cannot see the edge. But the machine can feel it. The motor that drives the table works harder as the edge goes blunt: near the end, up to two point seven times its starting current. And the vibration sensors, listening twenty-five thousand times a second, hear a new beat. Once per turn. The sound of a chipped tooth.
s06_bits

To a computer, that sound is only numbers. Sample the wave, and every instant becomes a number. Every number becomes bits. One cut becomes five sensors, times four thousand and ninety-six readings. One cutter's life becomes millions of them.
s07_autoencoder

Our first network is an autoencoder. It squeezes twenty thousand numbers through a bottleneck of just sixty-four, then tries to rebuild the original. We trained it only on healthy cutting. So when a worn tool sounds different, the rebuild fails. And the size of that failure becomes a health score.
s08_tcn

Our second network reads the cutter's history like a sentence. A temporal convolutional network. Each layer looks twice as far into the past: one, two, four, eight cycles back. Never into the future. After every cycle, it draws a risk curve: the chance of breaking on each cycle still to come.
s09_honesty

Then we tried to fool ourselves, and caught it. We hid one whole cutter at a time, so the model was always judged on a tool it had never seen. We raced our network against thirty others: trees, recurrent nets, transformers, convolutions on raw sound. The good ones finished within the noise of each other. With thirteen cutters, the limit is not the model. It is the data.
s10_decision

And then, the decision. After every cycle, weigh the chance of breaking, times the cost of a breakage, against the cost of changing the tool right now. When the risk outweighs the cost, change it. Replayed on thirteen real cutters, that rule let five break, instead of ten.
s11_close
Steel, to signals, to numbers, to a choice. The tool will always break. The only question is whether you see it coming. ToolLife Policy.
